passages.t: Refugees at Zion's door, and a throne in the tent of David
passages.happening:
‘Send the tribute lambs to the ruler of the land, from Sela in the desert to the mount of Daughter Zion’ (verse 1). Like birds pushed out of the nest, ‘so are the daughters of Moab at the fords of the Arnon’ (verse 2).

The refugees plead: give counsel, make a decision, shelter them at noon with shade as dark as night, hide the fugitives and do not betray those who flee (verse 3). Let Moab's fugitives stay, and be a refuge from the destroyer (verse 4).

When the oppressor is gone and destruction has ended, ‘in loving devotion a throne will be established in the tent of David. A judge seeking justice and hastening righteousness will sit on it in faithfulness’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 15 mourned a disaster sweeping through Moab. Chapter 16 adds a new thought: could Moab find refuge with Judah and its God?

Verse 1 recalls an old arrangement. When Moab was subject to Israel in the ninth century BC, its king Mesha paid a heavy tribute of lambs and wool. Now the oracle pictures Moab sending lambs again, this time to Jerusalem, as the price of protection. Sela, meaning rock, may be a place in Edom or simply a rocky refuge in the desert. The fords of the Arnon were the crossings of the deep gorge that formed Moab's northern boundary.

The refugees' plea is moving: shade at noon as dark as night, a hiding place, no betrayal. The answer points to a just king from David's line, in the language of the promises of chapters 9 and 11. His throne is built on loving devotion, chesed, and he hurries to do right. The first hearers were shown a Zion that could shelter even its old enemies, if they came.
passages.later: Long before, a Moabite woman had come to Bethlehem and said, ‘your people will be my people, and your God will be my God’ (Ruth 1:16). Amos promises, ‘In that day I will restore the fallen tent of David’ (Amos 9:11), and James quotes that promise when Gentiles come to faith (Acts 15:16).
passages.asks: The refugees ask for shade, a hiding place and no betrayal. Ask how your community treats people who come fleeing. And ask what it means that God's king is pictured as a refuge even for those who were once enemies.

passages.t: Moab's pride, and a prophet who weeps
passages.happening:
‘We have heard of Moab’s pomposity, his exceeding pride and conceit, his overflowing arrogance. But his boasting is empty’ (verse 6).

So let Moab wail, and moan for the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth (verse 7). The fields of Heshbon have withered, and the vines of Sibmah, which once spread to Jazer and the desert and beyond the sea, have been trampled by the rulers of the nations (verse 8).

Then the prophet weeps: ‘So I weep with Jazer for the vines of Sibmah; I drench Heshbon and Elealeh with my tears’ (verse 9). Joy is gone from the orchards; no one sings in the vineyards or treads the grapes (verse 10). ‘Therefore my heart laments for Moab like a harp, my inmost being for Kir-heres’ (verse 11).

When Moab wears itself out at the high place and goes into its sanctuary to pray, it will do no good (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Moab's pride was famous. What blocks the way to refuge is not God's refusal but Moab's arrogance.

Moab was known for its vineyards, and its vines were the pride of the land. Raisin cakes were pressed cakes of dried grapes, eaten at festivals and offered in worship. The harvest season should have been full of singing as the grapes were trodden. Now it is silent.

The prophet weeps. His heart sounds like a harp's lament. The first hearers were being taught to grieve even over a proud enemy brought low.

Verse 12 adds that Moab's prayers at its high place will not help. Its gods cannot save it.
passages.later: Jeremiah repeats verse 6 nearly word for word in his own oracle on Moab: ‘We have heard of Moab’s pomposity, his exceeding pride and conceit’ (Jeremiah 48:29).
passages.asks: Moab's pride stood between it and refuge. Ask what pride stands between you and the help you need. And ask whether you can weep, as the prophet did, for people whose fall you might have expected to cheer.

passages.happening:
‘This is the message that the LORD spoke earlier concerning Moab’ (verse 13).

And now the LORD says, ‘In three years, as a hired worker counts the years, Moab’s splendor will become an object of contempt, with all her many people. And those who are left will be few and feeble’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
These two verses are a prose note. They say that the oracle was spoken earlier and now receives a timetable: in three years. A hired worker counts the years of his contract exactly, no more and no less.

The occasion is uncertain. Assyria campaigned in the region repeatedly in the late eighth century BC, and Sennacherib's records from 701 BC list the king of Moab among the rulers who submitted and brought him gifts. Some scholars link the three years to Assyrian pressure under Sargon II around 715 to 711 BC, others to Sennacherib's campaign, and others leave it unidentified.

The note shows how prophetic words were remembered and applied again. An older oracle is reaffirmed with a new date. Jeremiah later does the same with much of this material, and Moab faded as an independent people after the Babylonian era.
passages.later: Jeremiah's oracle on Moab ends with a promise as well as a judgment: the LORD will restore Moab ‘from captivity’ in the latter days (Jeremiah 48:47).
passages.hard:
Did the three-year prophecy of verse 14 come true, and how would anyone know?

The honest answer is that the three years cannot be identified with certainty, because the text does not say when verse 13 was spoken. Assyrian records show that Moab submitted to Assyria more than once in the late eighth century BC, including in 701 BC, and some interpreters connect the prophecy with Sargon II's campaigns around 715 to 711 BC. Others note that the oracle speaks of Moab's splendor becoming contemptible and its survivors few, a humiliation that could come through defeat and heavy tribute rather than destruction.

Readers who expect prophecy to name dates and outcomes precisely may find this frustrating. What the text does show is that Israel kept and applied prophetic words again when they were renewed for a new moment, and that later readers, Jeremiah among them, treated them as still living.
passages.asks: An old word from God was renewed with a timetable. Ask whether there is a word God spoke to you long ago that you have forgotten. And ask what it means to trust God's timing when you cannot see how it is being kept.
